feasible

FEE-zuh-bul — starts like 'fee'; a feasible plan doesn't cost more effort than it's worth. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Feasible is capable of being done, achieved, or carried out successfully.

After running the numbers twice, the accountant confirmed the expansion plan was financially feasible.

Example

A group of students wants to build a working robot for the science fair in just two weeks. An engineer reviews their plan, checks the parts list and timeline, and tells them it is feasible if they start immediately.

The plan can actually be carried out with the time and resources they really have. Unlike 'ideal,' which describes the best possible option, feasible simply means the plan is realistically doable.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

achievable: Achievable describes a goal that is within reach with the effort and means available — a sales target, a grade, a personal best. Feasible describes the plan for getting there, judged realistic after someone checks the time, money, and resources. A goal is achievable; the plan to reach it is feasible.

workable: Workable means practical enough to actually be used — a workable compromise, a workable schedule. It cares about whether something functions day to day. Feasible is the verdict of an evaluation: after the budget, time, and resources are checked, the plan is judged doable. A rough idea can be workable before anyone has shown it is feasible.

practicable: Practicable is the formal twin of feasible: capable of being done in practice. The shade of difference is that practicable asks only whether a thing can physically and practically be done, while feasible usually adds whether it is realistic given costs and time. Lawyers write practicable; planners say feasible.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

doomed: certain to fail from the start

unattainable: impossible to achieve

Where it sits · how certain success is

possible → feasible → guaranteed

possible vs. feasible: Possible is weaker than feasible — something possible could theoretically happen, while something feasible has actually been checked and judged realistic given real resources and time.

guaranteed vs. feasible: Guaranteed is stronger than feasible: a feasible plan is realistically doable, but a guaranteed one is certain to succeed, with no doubt at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — feas: to do, to make (from Old French fais-, the stem of faire, from Latin facere 'to do, to make')

Suffix — -ible: able to be (Latin)

Put it together: Feas ('to do, to make' -- Old French fais-, from Latin facere) + -ible ('able to be') spell feasible: able to be done -- literally 'do-able.'

Use the root in a new word: manufacture: The factory used robots to manufacture thousands of identical parts every day.
